deed: מדעני מכון ויצמן פיתחו את קופקסון — תרופה ישראלית לטרשת נפוצה שאישרה ה-FDA
title: Three Weizmann Institute researchers developed Copaxone, a multiple sclerosis drug approved in dozens of countries

trailer.text: Prof. Michael Sela, an Israeli scientist whose research led to the development of drugs for cancer and multiple sclerosis, worked at the Weizmann Institute in Rehovot with Prof. Ruth Arnon and Dr. Dvora Teitelbaum.
In 1967 the three tried to trigger symptoms of multiple sclerosis in lab animals by injecting synthetic proteins.
Surprisingly, instead of causing the disease, the substances blocked a multiple sclerosis-like disease in mice.
One of them became the drug Copaxone, produced by the Israeli company Teva.
According to the Telegraph, the drug was approved for use in the US in 1996, and it has been approved for use in dozens of countries, including Britain.

stations.title: Before: a disease and a lab in Rehovot

paragraphs.text: Multiple sclerosis is an autoimmune disease.
The immune system erroneously attacks the myelin coating that protects nerve fibers in the central nervous system.
Because of the disease, body movement becomes difficult, and partial or complete paralysis may develop.
According to a 1996 Weizmann Institute press release, about one million people worldwide then had MS, some 300,000 of them in the US and another 350,000 in Europe.
The Weizmann Institute is a center of research and higher education in Rehovot.
In 1963 Michael Sela founded the Chemical Immunology Section there.
In the late 1960s Arnon, Sela and Teitelbaum synthesized molecules known as copolymers.
They hoped to create an animal model for studying multiple sclerosis.
In 1967 they injected the synthetic proteins into lab animals in order to trigger disease symptoms in them.
The researchers were surprised: not a single animal that received the molecules developed multiple sclerosis.
Sela said that only about a year and a half later did it occur to them that if the molecules did not cause the disease, perhaps they cured it.
According to Sela in an interview, the drug was developed by accident.

stations.title: A lab substance against a disease

paragraphs.text: Arnon and Sela succeeded in synthesizing in the laboratory a substance that aroused the immune system, the first synthetic antigen.
Together with Dvora Teitelbaum, they discovered that such a synthetic substance could suppress in animals a disease that serves as a model for multiple sclerosis.
According to the press release, the drug also triggers the production of immune-system suppressor cells.
These cells inhibit the action of the attacking cells.
The drug was first investigated in humans at Hadassah-Hebrew University in Jerusalem and at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York.
Yeda, the company that commercializes Weizmann Institute research, granted the Israeli company Teva exclusive worldwide rights to manufacture and market the drug.
According to Globes, the agreement with Teva was signed relatively late, after the drug had passed a human feasibility trial, and the Institute retained a significant share of the proceeds.
According to the press release, Teva further developed the drug with physicians and researchers from Israel and other countries.
In a decisive double-blind trial, between 1991 and 1994, the drug was tested on several hundred patients in eleven hospitals in the US.
A request for marketing approval was filed with the FDA in the year before the approval.
Almost thirty years of research and experimentation passed between the discovery and the approval.
According to the Weizmann Institute press release, the FDA approved copolymer-1, to be marketed under the name Copaxone, for patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis.
According to the Telegraph, this happened in 1996.
The drug was approved for marketing in Israel, the US and Europe.
According to the press release, in trials the drug reduced the number of attacks and improved the condition of patients in early stages.
According to the press release, it produces almost no negative side effects.
According to the Telegraph, it did not cure the disease, but it made attacks less frequent and reduced disability in the long run.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, Copaxone allows patients to lead near-normal lives.
According to the Telegraph, Copaxone has been approved in dozens of countries.
Billions of dollars went to Teva, which for many years held the exclusive manufacturing rights.
According to Globes, it was the first non-generic product that Teva purchased.
According to reports, Yeda received 8%-9% of the sales, around $2 billion.
Copaxone is considered one of the great successes of the Israeli pharmaceutical industry.
In 1998 Sela and Arnon shared the Wolf Prize in Medicine.
Arnon won the Israel Prize for medicine in 2001.
Sela won the Israel Prize already at the age of 35.
Arnon told Haaretz that Sela developed the entire field of immunology in Israel.
Rising antisemitism drove his family to Romania and then to Palestine, where he arrived at age 17.
From 1975 to 1985 he served as president of the Weizmann Institute.
According to the Jewish Press, he held the patents on Copaxone and on Erbitux, used to treat cancer.
Ruth Arnon is an Israeli immunologist at the Weizmann Institute.
She was born in Tel Aviv on June 1, 1933.
In 1957 she became Sela's first doctoral student.
Arnon holds the Paul Ehrlich Chair of Immunology, and Sela held the W. Garfield Weston Chair.
Sela is known as the co-developer of Copaxone with Arnon and Teitelbaum.
According to the Telegraph, on February 28, 1924
According to Globes, a dispute between the Weizmann Institute and Teva went to arbitration, which the Institute won.
Globes reports a claim that Yeda plays legal hardball, and Yeda's head, Naiberg, rejects it.
According to Globes, Copaxone's US patents expired on 24 May 2014.

versions.says: The Telegraph (Sela obituary, 2022): the drug made relapses less frequent and reduced disability in the long run.
Cochrane review (2010): partly effective against relapses, but with no significant effect on sustained disability progression.
